paragraphs: The paper studies how well k-means++ and the broader family of D^ℓ sampling algorithms can initialize a clustering. Its central question is what happens when an algorithm may select more than the requested k centers. This changes the comparison: the algorithm receives extra centers, but its clustering quality is still judged against the best solution using only k.

The result allows any fixed multiplier β greater than one. Selecting βk centers gives an expected clustering cost within a constant factor of the optimal k-center cost, without imposing conditions on the dataset. The guarantee is therefore about average performance over the sampling randomness, rather than a promise about every individual run.

This is a bi-criteria approximation because it trades additional centers for a stronger cost guarantee. With exactly k centers, the previously known bound grew logarithmically with k. The new result establishes a constant-factor bound when extra centers are allowed, and strengthens an earlier bi-criteria result that held only with constant probability.
neurips-2016-a-constant-factor-bi-criter.tldr: Allowing a constant-factor increase in centers gives D^ℓ sampling a constant-factor expected approximation to optimal k-center clustering.

paragraphs: Sequential decision methods must decide both what conclusion to draw and when enough evidence has arrived. The number of observations can depend on earlier observations, so it is itself random. This makes reliable uncertainty guarantees a central part of deciding when to stop collecting data.

The paper introduces concentration inequalities resembling Hoeffding bounds that remain valid for an adaptively chosen sample count. These inequalities control how far sample-based quantities can deviate while accommodating the way the decision process chooses its own amount of evidence. The authors establish tightness under natural assumptions, making the assumptions part of the stated theoretical claim.

The bounds are applied to sequential hypothesis testing, identifying the best arm, and sorting. Across these applications, the resulting algorithms match or improve on the state of the art in theory and experiments. The contribution is also methodological: a shared uncertainty tool can simplify analyses that would otherwise need to handle adaptive sampling separately for each decision problem.
neurips-2016-adaptive-concentration-ineq.tldr: New concentration bounds support reliable decisions when the number of samples is chosen adaptively.

paragraphs: A sequence model that conditions its outputs on the complete input cannot naturally respond while that input is still arriving. The paper introduces a Neural Transducer that produces predictions incrementally, using the input observed so far and the output already generated. It can continue processing without repeating the entire computation.

At each time step, the model may emit no symbols, one symbol, or several symbols. An encoder can first process the data before passing it to the transducer. This arrangement gives the model flexibility over when to produce output, rather than requiring a fixed correspondence between incoming data and emitted symbols.

Choosing whether to emit a symbol is discrete, which makes conventional backpropagation difficult. The authors address this by using dynamic programming to generate target decisions for training. Experiments show that the model works well when predictions must arrive alongside incoming data. They also report good performance on long sequences without attention mechanisms, supporting the usefulness of partial conditioning in those tested settings.
neurips-2016-an-online-sequence-to-seque.tldr: The Neural Transducer learns to emit outputs from partially observed inputs, enabling incremental prediction without repeating the full computation.

paragraphs: Probabilistic programs describe models through code containing sampled variables. This paper presents a general framework for marginal maximum a posteriori estimation: optimizing selected variables while accounting for uncertainty in others through marginalization. The aim is to make this optimization available across probabilistic programs rather than requiring a separate method for each model.

A sequence of code transformations makes the program's evidence optimizable with respect to an arbitrary subset of sampled variables. The authors then develop a Bayesian optimization package that directly uses the target program's source code. That access supports methods for problem-independent hyperpriors, searching unbounded domains, and satisfying constraints implicitly.

The important connection is between model representation and optimization: the program supplies structure that the optimizer can exploit. The abstract reports significant performance improvements over prominent existing packages and describes applications including engineering design and parameter optimization. It presents the framework as the first general-purpose approach of its kind, with the same program-based formulation extending to graphical models.
neurips-2016-bayesian-optimization-for-p.tldr: A Bayesian optimization framework exploits probabilistic program source code to optimize selected variables while marginalizing others.

paragraphs: Constrained optimization asks for a good solution that also satisfies requirements. An augmented Lagrangian handles this by turning the original task into a sequence of simpler optimization problems. Bayesian optimization can solve these subproblems using surrogate models, supporting a more global search than the local solvers typically used in this framework.

An earlier combination of these ideas handled inequality constraints, but evaluating its expected improvement criterion required Monte Carlo calculations. This paper introduces an alternative formulation using slack variables. In the new formulation, expected improvement can be evaluated through library routines, changing how the search criterion is computed.

The slack variables also allow the method to accommodate equality constraints, inequality constraints, and mixtures of both. This matters because mixed requirements can be handled within the same optimization construction. The authors report that their slack-variable ALBO method compares favorably with the original approach. Additional mixed-constraint examples reinforce its reported advantage over conventional alternatives in the evaluated problems.
neurips-2016-bayesian-optimization-under.tldr: A slack-variable formulation extends augmented-Lagrangian Bayesian optimization to mixed constraints and simplifies expected improvement evaluation.

paragraphs: Helpfulness votes are intended to identify useful reviews and answers, but they are also part of a social process. Existing popularity and the direction of previous votes can influence subsequent voting. A response's accumulated votes therefore reflect both its quality and the circumstances under which people encounter and judge it.

The paper introduces the Chinese Voting Process to model how these votes evolve. Voting is represented as self-reinforcing, with position and presentation biases affecting the process. This makes the history and display of responses relevant to the model, allowing it to represent momentum rather than treating all votes as interchangeable observations.

The authors evaluate the model using Amazon product reviews and more than 80 StackExchange forums. They use it to measure the intrinsic quality of individual responses and behavioral coefficients for different communities. The contribution is a framework for interpreting helpfulness votes through an explicit model of social influence, with response quality and community voting behavior represented as distinct aspects of the observed process.
neurips-2016-beyond-exchangeability-the-.tldr: The Chinese Voting Process models helpfulness votes as a socially reinforced process shaped by response position and presentation.

paragraphs: Convolutional neural networks can require substantial storage and computation, making deployment on mobile devices difficult. CNNpack addresses both costs by representing convolutional filters in the frequency domain. Its compression strategy considers relationships among filters as well as the weights within each filter.

The method treats filters as images and separates their frequency representations into shared and individual components. Similar filters share a common cluster-center representation, while residuals capture their differences. Many low-energy frequency coefficients can then be removed from both components. The abstract reports that this produces strong compression without significantly compromising accuracy.

CNNpack also reduces convolutional computation by linearly combining responses of discrete cosine transform bases. This connects the compressed representation to a way of performing the network's operations with less computational burden. The paper analyzes compression and speed-up ratios and evaluates them on benchmark image datasets, reporting advantages over state-of-the-art methods. Its central idea is to use frequency structure for both compact storage and more efficient computation.
neurips-2016-cnnpack-packing-convolution.tldr: CNNpack compresses shared and individual filter structure in the frequency domain and uses DCT basis responses to reduce convolution costs.

paragraphs: Online learning algorithms make decisions repeatedly and are judged by regret: how much worse they perform than a comparison strategy. Choosing a learning rate can be difficult when the best choice depends on an unknown competitor. Parameter-free methods seek strong regret guarantees without requiring that information to tune their updates.

This paper develops a common design framework for online linear optimization over Hilbert spaces and learning with expert advice. It reduces these tasks to betting on adversarial coin outcomes. The betting formulation provides a way to construct learning algorithms through another sequential decision problem, rather than choosing learning rates using unavailable knowledge.

The authors instantiate the framework with a betting algorithm based on the Krichevsky–Trofimov estimator. The resulting learning algorithms are simple and require no parameter tuning. Their regret guarantees and computational cost per round improve on or match previous results. The contribution is therefore both a reusable construction and concrete algorithms that retain competitive theoretical guarantees without oracle-selected learning rates.
neurips-2016-coin-betting-and-parameter-.tldr: Reducing online learning to adversarial coin betting yields simple algorithms with competitive regret bounds and no tuning parameters.

paragraphs: Dense image segmentation involves deciding how many small image elements should be grouped into coherent regions. These decisions interact, making the problem combinatorial. CELIS addresses that structure by using a neural network to assign an energy to a proposed segmentation conditioned on the image.

The paper provides efficient algorithms both for learning this energy function and for locally optimizing it. The search operates over agglomerations of supervoxels, meaning combinations of small three-dimensional image regions. This connects a learned assessment of the segmentation with a procedure for changing its grouping, so the model directly addresses the space of possible region combinations.

Evaluation uses a public three-dimensional microscopy dataset containing 25 billion voxels of ground truth. On an 11 billion voxel test set, CELIS improves volumetric reconstruction accuracy by more than 20% over two state-of-the-art baselines. Those baselines use CNN boundary predictions with graph-based segmentation, or a random forest to merge CNN-generated supervoxels. The result supports the value of learned combinatorial energies for this reconstruction setting.
neurips-2016-combinatorial-energy-learni.tldr: CELIS learns segmentation energies and locally optimizes supervoxel groupings, improving reconstruction accuracy on a large microscopy test set.

paragraphs: Many statistical tasks require a quantity derived from a probability density, such as an entropy or divergence, rather than the entire density itself. This paper analyzes a general family of estimators that use nearest-neighbor statistics to estimate such quantities for continuous distributions without specifying a parametric density model.

A conventional route first estimates the density consistently and then inserts that estimate into the desired functional. In the nearest-neighbor setting described here, that route requires the neighbor count k to grow with the sample size. The studied estimators instead keep k fixed and correct for bias, targeting the functional through this different construction.

The authors provide guarantees for finite samples, unifying several earlier estimators within one framework. For most of those estimators, these are the first such guarantees. They also show that keeping k fixed with bias correction can offer computational and statistical benefits, including faster convergence rates. The result clarifies why estimating a density-derived quantity need not follow the same strategy as estimating the full density.
neurips-2016-finite-sample-analysis-of-f.tldr: Finite-sample guarantees show how fixed-k nearest-neighbor statistics with bias correction can efficiently estimate entropies and divergences.

paragraphs: Crowdsourcing combines many small contributions from workers whose answers may be imperfect. A central design question is how much accuracy a fixed budget can buy, considering both the questions sent to workers and the procedure used to interpret their responses. This paper studies that trade-off through information theory.

The authors formulate crowdsourcing within a rate-distortion framework, which connects resource constraints with achievable reconstruction fidelity. Workers are modeled as parallel noisy channels. A joint source-channel coding and decoding construction represents the query scheme and the inference procedure, bringing both parts of the crowdsourcing process into the same analysis.

The goal is to characterize the ultimate fidelity attainable under the model for a given budget across query and decoding choices. Beyond these fundamental limits, the paper presents and analyzes a specific query method called k-ary incidence coding and studies optimized query pricing. The approach makes worker imperfection, query design, inference, and spending parts of one mathematical problem rather than treating accuracy as a property of aggregation alone.
neurips-2016-fundamental-limits-of-budge.tldr: An information-theoretic model characterizes the budget–accuracy trade-off in crowdsourcing and analyzes query coding and pricing.

paragraphs: Predicting a physical system requires reasoning about individual objects and how they affect one another. The interaction network makes this organization explicit by taking a graph as input and using deep neural networks for object-centered and relation-centered reasoning. Its computations resemble a simulation while remaining learnable.

The model supports both predictions of changing physical states and inference about broader system properties. The authors evaluate it on n-body interactions, rigid-body collisions, and non-rigid dynamics. These domains test whether the same general approach can represent different kinds of physical relationships rather than only one narrowly specified interaction.

The reported results show accurate learned trajectories for dozens of objects across thousands of time steps, alongside estimates of abstract quantities such as energy. The model also generalizes to systems with different numbers and configurations of objects and relations. The authors present the implementation as the first general-purpose learnable physics engine. The findings support graph-organized reasoning as a way to learn dynamics that transfer across changes in system composition.
neurips-2016-interaction-networks-for-le.tldr: Interaction networks use graph-based object and relation reasoning to learn physical dynamics and generalize across system configurations.

paragraphs: Weighted nearest-neighbor methods estimate a value or class using nearby examples, but two choices strongly shape the prediction: how many neighbors to include and how much influence each receives. This paper addresses those choices together through a local regression and classification approach that explicitly represents the bias–variance trade-off.

The formulation defines what optimal weights mean within that trade-off and provides an efficient way to find them. It also selects the number of neighbors adaptively for each point being estimated. Thus, the neighborhood size and weighting can change across the data instead of being settled through one shared choice for every prediction.

This local adaptation matters because choosing neighbors and assigning their weights are connected decisions: changing which examples participate changes the available weighting problem. The paper offers a simple formulation that handles both within the same optimization. Experiments on several datasets demonstrate applicability and report better performance than standard locally weighted methods, providing empirical support for the proposed way of balancing local estimation errors.
neurips-2016-k-nearest-neighbors-from-gl.tldr: An explicit bias–variance formulation adaptively selects neighbor counts and weights for each regression or classification prediction.

paragraphs: Visual markers encode information that must survive being fabricated and photographed. This paper learns both sides of that process: one deep network converts bit strings into color images, and another recovers the bits from photographs of those images. Marker design becomes a joint learning problem between an encoder and a reader.

The networks are trained together using backpropagation while accounting for photometric and geometric distortions associated with production and capture. An optional stylization loss uses activation statistics from a pretrained classification network to move the marker's appearance toward a chosen texture. Information encoding and visual appearance can therefore be shaped within the same training process.

Experiments show that the learned markers retain bit strings long enough to be practically useful. The approach can adapt to a usage scenario and desired capacity while also incorporating artistic stylization. The authors additionally use it to investigate patterns that convolutional networks recognize effectively and their ability to distinguish composite patterns, connecting marker generation with questions about learned visual recognition.
neurips-2016-learnable-visual-markers-5e.tldr: Jointly trained networks create and read visual markers that can adapt to capture conditions, information capacity, and artistic style.

paragraphs: A useful embedding should assign greater similarity to matching examples than to non-matching examples. This paper turns that ordering goal into a training loss by comparing two distributions: similarity scores for positive pairs and similarity scores for negative pairs. The objective measures how often their ordering goes the wrong way.

Specifically, the loss estimates the probability that a positive pair receives a lower similarity than a negative pair. The authors compute this through one-dimensional histograms with soft assignments. These operations are simple and piecewise differentiable, allowing the loss to be used in stochastic optimization when training a deep embedding network.

The loss itself has no tunable parameters, reducing the need to select settings for the training criterion. Experiments across multiple datasets and problems show favorable results compared with recently proposed losses. The contribution is a distribution-based way to express the desired separation between matching and non-matching pairs, together with a histogram construction that makes that objective usable in neural-network training.
neurips-2016-learning-deep-embeddings-wi.tldr: Histogram loss trains embeddings by estimating how often non-matching pairs appear more similar than matching pairs.

paragraphs: The paper models social influence using an Ising system at dynamic equilibrium, with individual opinions represented as spins. Influence maximization becomes the problem of allocating a limited external magnetic field to maximize magnetization. This gives the allocation problem a physical formulation suited to opinions that remain part of an ongoing equilibrium process.

Under a mean-field approximation, the authors develop a gradient ascent algorithm that uses susceptibility to efficiently find local maxima. They also establish sufficient conditions under which mean-field magnetization is concave and the algorithm converges to a global optimum. Those global guarantees depend on the conditions and concern the mean-field formulation.

Experiments on random and real-world networks reveal a phase transition in the optimal mean-field allocations. At high temperatures, influence focuses on high-degree individuals; at low temperatures, it shifts toward low-degree individuals. This shows that the preferred targets can change with the model's regime. The paper also establishes structural results about steady states of ferromagnetic mean-field Ising systems on general graphs.
neurips-2016-maximizing-influence-in-an-.tldr: A mean-field Ising influence algorithm has conditional global guarantees and reveals temperature-dependent shifts in whom to target.

paragraphs: Training a network to estimate three-dimensional human pose requires images paired with three-dimensional annotations, which are scarce for unconstrained scenes. This paper generates additional training examples by combining real images carrying two-dimensional pose labels with three-dimensional motion-capture data. The resulting synthetic images retain known three-dimensional pose annotations.

For a candidate motion-capture pose, the synthesis engine projects it into two dimensions and selects source images with locally matching poses around each joint. It then stitches image patches together under kinematic constraints. The generated data trains an end-to-end CNN, with poses clustered into many classes so that pose estimation becomes a classification problem supported by the large training set.

The method surpasses the state of the art on Human3.6M, a controlled-environment dataset, and produces promising results on unconstrained LSP images. These findings support the reported transfer from artificial training images to real photographs. The distinction between the stronger controlled-setting result and the promising in-the-wild result is important to the scope of the evidence.
neurips-2016-mocap-guided-data-augmentat.tldr: Motion-capture-guided patch synthesis creates annotated training images that improve CNN-based three-dimensional human pose estimation.

paragraphs: Music transcription can be approached by decomposing an audio spectrogram into representative note spectra. Conventional fit measures compare individual frequency entries, so small movements of energy between bins or changes in timbre can make a reasonable match appear poor. The paper changes how the observed and template spectra are compared.

Its proposed measure uses optimal transportation to treat spectral energy as a distribution across frequencies. Incorporating the harmonic structure of sound makes the measure invariant to energy shifts between harmonically related frequencies and to small local displacements. The comparison therefore accounts for relationships among frequencies rather than relying only on entry-by-entry agreement.

This measure also simplifies the note dictionary. Full spectral templates can be replaced by Dirac vectors concentrated at the target fundamental frequencies, or musical pitches. That simplification supports a fast and simple decomposition algorithm. The authors report state-of-the-art performance on real musical data, showing how a more suitable notion of spectral fit can reduce the complexity of the representation used for transcription.
neurips-2016-optimal-spectral-transporta.tldr: A transport-based spectral fit measure enables simplified note templates and fast music transcription with state-of-the-art reported performance.

paragraphs: A protein contact map records which pairs of amino acids are close in its three-dimensional structure. Because structure is closely related to function, predicting these contacts can help address biological questions. This paper uses a convolutional network to infer contact maps from statistical couplings between positions in a protein sequence.

The input resembles an image because information is arranged across pairs of sequence positions. However, each location contains a bipartite, undirected, weighted graph rather than ordinary color channels. The authors propose several ways for convolutional networks to process these graph-valued images, preserving a richer kind of information at each position in the input.

The proposed method is reported to outperform state-of-the-art contact prediction methods by a large margin. Its input representation also permits substantial flexibility in the data supplied to the network. The broader contribution is therefore a way to connect convolutional processing with image-like arrays whose entries have graph structure, alongside the demonstrated application to predicting protein contacts from inferred sequence couplings.
neurips-2016-protein-contact-prediction-.tldr: Convolutional networks process graph-valued sequence-coupling inputs to predict protein contacts with a large reported improvement over existing methods.

paragraphs: Adversarial bandit algorithms must make repeated choices under limited feedback, and regret measures their disadvantage relative to a comparison arm. This paper studies unavoidable regret through lower bounds. Such results establish how much room remains to improve an algorithm's guarantees, rather than proposing another decision rule.

The new bounds show that several recent upper guarantees are close to tight. These include guarantees that hold with high probability, depend on the total loss of the best arm, or depend on the quadratic variation of the losses. The results therefore support the sharpness of multiple ways of describing problem difficulty.

The authors also establish two impossibility results. Having one arm that is optimal in every round does not improve worst-case regret, and regret cannot scale with the effective range of the losses. Both kinds of improvement are possible with full information. This contrast identifies a substantive consequence of bandit feedback: favorable loss structure need not translate into the same guarantees available when all losses are observed.
neurips-2016-refined-lower-bounds-for-ad.tldr: New lower bounds show several adversarial bandit guarantees are nearly tight and rule out two improvements available with full information.

paragraphs: Recommending relevant labels becomes difficult when training labels are missing and evaluation uses a metric such as F1. Such a metric evaluates the selected labels jointly rather than adding independent scores for each label. The paper addresses missing supervision and the desired evaluation criterion within one framework.

Given a performance metric, the framework constructs a regularized training objective and a threshold for selecting positive predictions from a score vector. The analysis connects regret in that metric to errors in estimating underlying parameters. It provides precise finite-sample bounds for collaborative filtering, multilabel classification, and positive-unlabeled learning, with bounds that can remain small even when many labels are missing.

Experiments on synthetic and benchmark datasets report significantly better performance, including F1, than methods that do not carefully model missing labels. The findings support jointly designing training and prediction around the actual metric and incomplete observations. The theoretical contribution explains how parameter estimation quality translates into the performance measure that ultimately determines whether the selected labels are useful.
neurips-2016-regret-bounds-for-non-decom.tldr: A framework combines missing-label modeling with metric-specific training and thresholding, backed by finite-sample regret bounds.

paragraphs: Convolutional networks benefit from labeled training data, but obtaining large labeled collections is costly. The paper studies semi-supervised learning, where unlabeled examples also contribute to training. Its approach builds on the randomness already present in techniques such as data augmentation, dropout, and random max-pooling.

Because these techniques are stochastic, passing the same example through the network several times can produce different predictions. The authors introduce an unsupervised loss that minimizes those differences. Multiple evaluations of one example thereby supply a training signal based on agreement, without requiring a known label for that example.

The key idea is to use prediction variability under stochastic processing as something training can explicitly reduce. This gives unlabeled data a role in shaping the classifier while making use of techniques already associated with generalization and stability. The paper evaluates the approach on several benchmark datasets. Its stated contribution is the consistency loss and its evaluation, with the abstract making no specific claim about the size of a performance improvement.
neurips-2016-regularization-with-stochas.tldr: An unsupervised consistency loss trains a network to agree across repeated stochastic passes of the same example.

paragraphs: Structured prediction models are often trained by maximum likelihood but evaluated using a task-specific reward. This paper introduces a simple, computationally efficient way to bring that reward into likelihood training. The aim is to make the training signal reflect the quality of complete structured outputs.

The authors establish an approximate connection between maximum likelihood and regularized expected reward near an optimal solution. They then generalize likelihood training using auxiliary outputs sampled in proportion to exponentiated, scaled rewards. Reward therefore influences which alternative outputs receive training emphasis, connecting output augmentation with the evaluation objective.

The framework is applied to edit distance by sampling edited versions of target outputs. In experiments with neural sequence-to-sequence models for speech recognition and machine translation, this produces notable improvements over a maximum-likelihood baseline. The findings show that sampling target augmentations can provide a practical route for incorporating task reward. The theoretical equivalence remains local and approximate, while the reported gains come from the tested training procedure.
neurips-2016-reward-augmented-maximum-li.tldr: Reward-weighted sampling of alternative targets incorporates task reward into maximum-likelihood training and improves tested sequence prediction tasks.

paragraphs: Spectral methods seek global patterns through eigenvectors or singular vectors of a data matrix. In sparse or noisy data, those vectors can become localized, concentrating on a small part of the data instead of representing the broader structure. The paper addresses this failure by learning a regularization matrix from the localized eigenvectors themselves.

Matrix perturbation analysis shows how the learned regularization suppresses eigenvalues associated with localized directions. This enables recovery of informative eigenvectors that represent global structure. The method uses the unwanted spectral behavior to construct a correction, linking the diagnosis of localization with the modification applied to the matrix.

Applications include network community detection, clustering from pairwise similarities, rank estimation, and matrix completion. Extensive experiments show successful handling of localization and performance reaching theoretical detectability limits in different synthetic settings. The authors contrast these findings with poor sparse-noisy performance from several existing spectral constructions. Reaching those limits is an experimental finding in the studied synthetic data, rather than a universal claim for every input matrix.
neurips-2016-robust-spectral-detection-o.tldr: Learning regularization from localized eigenvectors helps spectral methods recover global structure in sparse or noisy data.

paragraphs: Recovering a signal from Gaussian noise is easier when its possible structure can be specified in advance. For a known convex, compact signal set, classical linear estimators can achieve risk within a constant factor of the minimax risk. The challenge considered here is recovery when that signal set is unspecified.

The paper proposes a family of estimators that does not require an explicit description of where the signal lives. Instead, it assumes that a well-performing linear estimator exists. This shifts the needed prior information from a declared structural set to the existence of an effective estimation rule, while leaving the proposed method blind to the hidden signal structure.

The estimators satisfy exact oracle inequalities, providing formal comparisons to the relevant oracle performance, and can be computed efficiently through convex optimization. Numerical illustrations show the approach's potential. The contribution combines a stated replacement assumption with both statistical guarantees and a tractable computation method, addressing how useful recovery remains possible without specifying the signal's structural class beforehand.
neurips-2016-structure-blind-signal-reco.tldr: Convexly computable estimators recover signals in Gaussian noise without a specified structural set, assuming a good linear estimator exists.
